The set itself is represented exactly: the body `{k | ∃ i, (i, k) ∈ PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSetUnion p n}` matches “`K_n = { k ∈ ℕ : ∃ i, (i,k) ∈ T'_n }`,” and `CoeffSupportSetUnion` correctly expands `T'_n` as the union over `Finset.range (n + 1)`, i.e. degrees `0` through `n`. However, the elaborated target adds the binder `[CommRing K]`, while the informal statement and supplied informal definitions never require that `K` be a commutative ring. This is a mathematically contentful restriction, not merely a decidability or notation instance. The restriction also enters through `PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSetUnion` and ultimately `PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSet`, both of which have `[CommRing K]`. To make the declaration faithful, either state in the blueprint that `K` is a commutative ring, or weaken the target and both dependencies consistently—at least to the weaker algebraic structure needed by the supplied `PowerSeries.coeff` interface, namely `[Semiring K]`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.lau.justification: Both target declarations faithfully encode the blueprint. The first uses `digits : ℕ →₀ ℤ`, whose definition already means all but finitely many values are zero, requires `∀ i, digits i ∈ btDigits` with `btDigits = {-1, 0, 1}`, and requires `∑ i ∈ digits.support, digits i * 3 ^ i = n`. This is equivalent to the blueprint’s `n = ∑_{i∈ℕ} b_i 3^i`; the reversed equality is immaterial. The second uses `digits : ℕ → BalancedTernaryDigit`, where the constructors and `toInt` encode exactly `{-1,0,1}`, requires `{i | digits i ≠ 0}.Finite`, exactly the stated meaning of “essentially finite,” and imposes `∑ᶠ i, (digits i).toInt * 3 ^ i = n`. Under that explicit finiteness hypothesis, `finsum` represents the required finite sum. Neither declaration adds a mathematically contentful restriction beyond the informal definition.

The blueprint defines a binary representation “of an integer $n$,” whereas the elaborated signature restricts the first binder to `ℕ`: `ℕ → Finset ℕ → Prop`. This excludes negative integers from the domain rather than assigning them no binary representations, so it is a mathematically contentful narrowing. The `Finset ℕ` encoding itself faithfully captures an essentially finite `{0,1}`-valued sequence via its support, and `n = ∑ i ∈ s, 2 ^ i` matches the stated sum under that encoding. To be faithful, change the target’s first binder to `n : ℤ` and interpret/coerce the finite sum of powers of two in `ℤ`, e.g. `n = ∑ i ∈ s, (2 : ℤ) ^ i`.

The body `fun K [Semiring K] => ℤ → K` identifies the type exactly with the blueprint’s carrier `K^{\mathbb Z}`: its elements are functions assigning an element of `K` to every integer, hence families `(a_n)_{n∈ℤ}`. The binder `[Semiring K]` is weaker than the blueprint setting inherited from `def.alg.module`, namely “Let `K` be a commutative ring”; thus it generalizes rather than restricts the intended setting. For every blueprint-eligible commutative ring, the definition still gives precisely `ℤ → K`. Since this is a reducible function type, its addition and scalar action are the usual pointwise operations, matching the two displayed formulas. The extra applicability to semirings and noncommutative semirings does not weaken the statement on the blueprint’s domain.

The formal declarations match all components of the blueprint. `LaurentPoly` has binder `(K : Type u_2) → [CommRing K]` and body `LaurentPolynomial K`, matching “Let K[x^{±}] … consist[] of all essentially finite families”; the supplied library meaning of Laurent polynomials/finitely supported functions captures exactly finite support. The indeterminate is defined by `laurentPoly_X ... => LaurentPolynomial.T 1`, matching `x = (δ_{i,1})_{i∈ℤ}`. Multiplication is stated as `(a * b) n = ∑ i ∈ a.support, a i * b (n - i)`, which is the finite-support realization of the blueprint’s `c_n = ∑_{i∈ℤ} a_i b_{n-i}`: indices outside `a.support` contribute zero. Finally, `laurentPolynomial_one_eq_T_zero` states `1 = LaurentPolynomial.T 0`; this is compatible with the multiplication and is even proved under the more general `[CommSemiring K]`, so it adds no restrictive hypothesis to the commutative-ring setting.

The predicate target exactly formalizes the defining condition. The blueprint says “all sufficiently low i ∈ ℤ satisfy a_i = 0,” while `IsLaurentSeries` has body `∃ N, ∀ n < N, f.coeff n = 0`. Since `DoublyInfinitePowerSeries K` is definitionally `ℤ → K` and `coeff f n` is `f n`, this is precisely bounded-below support, equivalently essential finiteness of `(a₋₁, a₋₂, …)`. Its binder `[Semiring K]` is weaker than the commutative-ring setting inherited from the blueprint’s definition of `K[[x^±]]` as a `K`-module, so this is a faithful generalization rather than an added restriction. The other target, `{K} → [CommRing K] → CommRing (LaurentSeries K)`, supplies an additional structural fact about Mathlib’s `LaurentSeries K`, whose base-library definition is stated to be a Hahn-series implementation; it imposes no hypothesis beyond the blueprint’s commutative-ring setting. Although its docstring calls this a commutative `K`-algebra while the signature only constructs a `CommRing`, the blueprint statement being judged does not require an algebra instance, so that wording does not create drift in the formalized definition.

The target quantifies over `{K : Type u_1} → [CommRing K] → (x : LaurentSeries K)` and constructs a `HahnSeries.SummableFamily ℤ K ↑(HahnSeries.support x)`, exactly corresponding to the claim that the monomials are indexed by `g ∈ supp(a)` and form a summable family. Its function is `fun ⟨g, _⟩ => (HahnSeries.single g) (x.coeff g)`; by the supplied docstring, `single g r` has coefficient `r` at `g` and zero elsewhere, so this is precisely the monomial `a_g · x^g`. `HahnSeries.SummableFamily` requires coefficientwise finite nonzero support and additionally that the union of supports is partially well-ordered, so inhabiting it implies the blueprint’s summability claim and supplies the condition needed for the sum to remain a Laurent/Hahn series. Although the section convention says that `K` is a commutative `ℚ`-algebra, the target assumes only `[CommRing K]`; this is a weaker hypothesis and therefore makes the construction strictly more general, which is faithful under the stated standard.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.lim.justification: The elaborated signature adds the mathematically substantive binder `[CommRing K]`, whereas the blueprint merely says “a sequence of FPSs over K” and defines an FPS as a sequence in `K^ℕ`; coefficientwise stabilization itself only uses coefficient extraction and equality. Thus the formal body correctly expresses `∀ n, ∃ N, ∀ i ≥ N, [x^n](f i) = [x^n]lim`, but only for commutative rings, excluding coefficient types for which the blueprint definition still makes sense. This restriction enters at the TARGET binder `[CommRing K]` (and operationally through `PowerSeries.coeff`, whose supplied signature requires `[Semiring K]`). To be faithful, the notion should be stated for arbitrary `K`, for example using the blueprint representation `ℕ → K` for FPSs or a coefficient accessor available without algebraic assumptions. Merely weakening `[CommRing K]` to `[Semiring K]` would improve generality but would still impose an assumption absent from the blueprint.

The coefficient conditions themselves match exactly: the formal body says “∀ i, constantCoeff (f i) = 1” and “∀ n, ∃ N, ∀ i ≥ N, ∀ k ≤ n, coeff k (f i) = if k = 0 then 1 else 0,” corresponding to clauses (1) and (2) and to δ_{k,0}. However, the elaborated signature adds the binder `[CommRing K]`, while the informal statement and its definitions only describe FPSs as sequences in `K^ℕ` and do not require K to be a commutative ring. This restricts the coefficient types and therefore weakens the definition's scope. The difference enters through the target declaration’s `[CommRing K]` binder. Since the supplied `PowerSeries.coeff` and `constantCoeff` APIs require only `[Semiring K]`, replacing `[CommRing K]` with `[Semiring K]` would remove the unnecessary commutativity and additive-inverse assumptions while retaining the available formal encoding.

The target takes a family `f : ℕ → PowerSeries K` and defines summability by `∀ (n : ℕ), {i | (PowerSeries.coeff n) (f i) ≠ 0}.Finite`. This exactly matches the blueprint: for every `n ∈ ℕ`, the set `{ i ∈ ℕ : [x^n] f_i ≠ 0 }` is finite. Here `PowerSeries.coeff n (f i)` is the `n`th coefficient `[x^n] f_i`, and the index type of the set is inferred from `i` as `ℕ`. The binder `[CommRing K]` supplies the coefficient-ring setting needed by `PowerSeries.coeff` and does not alter the stated finiteness condition.

The formal body `fun {K} a lim => ∃ N, ∀ i ≥ N, a i = lim` exactly matches the blueprint definition: for a sequence `a : ℕ → K` and value `lim : K`, “there exists some `N ∈ ℕ` such that all integers `i ≥ N` satisfy `a_i = a`.” The binders `(ℕ → K) → K → Prop` correctly encode a sequence in `K^ℕ` and its proposed eventual value, with no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The elaborated target adds the binder `[inst : CommRing K]`, while the blueprint only says “a multipliable family $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of FPSs” over an unspecified coefficient type `K`; none of the supplied informal definitions states that `K` is a commutative ring. This is a mathematically contentful restriction, not merely an encoding instance. It also enters through the dependency `PowerSeries.IsMultipliable`, whose signature likewise requires `[CommRing K]`. The actual multipliability condition matches the informal definition, and `Finset.range (N + 1)` correctly represents the product from `0` through `N`. To make the declaration faithful, the algebraic assumptions must be stated in the blueprint, or the target and `PowerSeries.IsMultipliable` should be weakened to the least structure needed—here, at least a commutative semiring for the supplied power-series and finite-product implementation.

The coefficientwise construction is correct: the body `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ∑ i ∈ … .toFinset, (PowerSeries.coeff n) (f i)` matches “the FPS … whose `n`-th coefficient is `∑_{i ∈ S_n} [x^n] f_i`,” and `PowerSeries.IsSummable` correctly makes each support set finite. However, the elaborated target adds the mathematically substantive binder `[inst : CommRing K]`, inherited also by `PowerSeries.IsSummable`, while the informal statement and definitions only describe FPSs as sequences over `K` and do not stipulate that `K` is a commutative ring. This narrows the allowed coefficient types and is not merely an encoding-only assumption. The blueprint construction can be stated under weaker structure; with the supplied `PowerSeries.coeff`, `[Semiring K]` suffices for coefficient extraction, zero, and finite sums. Changing both `PowerSeries.IsSummable` and `PowerSeries.tsum'` from `[CommRing K]` to `[Semiring K]` (or adding an explicit commutative-ring assumption to the blueprint) would remove the drift.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.lod.justification: The elaborated signature restricts coefficients to `{R : Type u_2} → [Field R]`, whereas the blueprint explicitly says “`K` can be an arbitrary commutative ring.” A field is a mathematically stronger, contentful hypothesis, so this omits non-field commutative rings and makes the formal definition weaker in scope. The body `derivative f * f⁻¹` matches `f′/f` for series with constant coefficient 1. Its accepting every `PowerSeries R`, rather than only `f ∈ K[[x]]₁`, is a harmless extension of the domain provided the intended restriction has the stated values. To make the declaration faithful, replace `[Field R]` by `[CommRing R]`, take a series together with `constantCoeff f = 1` (or the corresponding subtype), and construct its inverse from that unit condition rather than through `PowerSeries.instInv`, whose binder `[Field k]` is where the restrictive inverse operation enters.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.log.justification: The blueprint defines the series merely as an element of “K[[x]]” and does not state any hypothesis that K is a commutative ring or admits a rational-algebra structure. The elaborated target instead has the contentful binders “{K : Type u_1} → [inst : CommRing K] → [Algebra ℚ K] → PowerSeries K”. In particular, `[Algebra ℚ K]` restricts K to a commutative ℚ-algebra, excluding, for example, coefficient rings of positive characteristic; this is not just a decidability or presentation device. Under those added assumptions, the body is otherwise coefficientwise correct: it assigns 0 at n = 0 and maps `(-1)^(n-1) / n ∈ ℚ` into K for n ≠ 0, matching the displayed logarithm series and its zero constant term. To make the declaration faithful, the blueprint must explicitly assume that K is a commutative ℚ-algebra (or otherwise specify an equivalent coefficient setting supporting all the fractions 1/n). Conversely, if K is genuinely unrestricted in the blueprint, the formal dependency on `[Algebra ℚ K]` must be removed and the intended interpretation of those fractions over arbitrary K must first be supplied.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.mul.justification: Both target bodies formalize only part (a): `fun a => ∀ (n : ℕ), PowerSeries.CoeffFinitelyDeterminedInProd a n`. Through `CoeffFinitelyDeterminedInProd` and `DeterminesCoeffInProd`, this correctly expands to the existence, for every `n`, of a finite `M` such that every finite `J ⊇ M` has the same `x^n`-coefficient. However, the blueprint also contains part (b): “its product `∏_{i∈I} a_i` is defined to be the FPS” satisfying the displayed coefficient rule. Neither `PowerSeries.Multipliable` nor its alias introduces such an infinite-product FPS or states its coefficient specification. Thus the formal declarations do not imply the full informal statement. To make the package faithful, either scope the informal statement explicitly to part (a), or add a product declaration for multipliable families together with the part-(b) coefficient equation (and its well-definedness).

The blueprint denotes the formal power series algebra in k variables by K[[x₁,…,xₖ]], and the target defines `FPS k R` as `MvPowerSeries (Fin k) R`. The base-library descriptions identify `MvPowerSeries σ R` as multivariate formal power series indexed by σ and `Fin k` as the canonical k-element type, so this gives exactly k variables. Likewise, `BivFPS R := MvPowerSeries (Fin 2) R`, with `BivFPS.x := MvPowerSeries.X 0` and `BivFPS.y := MvPowerSeries.X 1`, faithfully realizes the two-variable notation and names. The formal binders use `[CommSemiring R]`, whereas the informal algebra definitions take K to be a commutative ring. This is a weaker hypothesis and hence a strictly more general construction; every commutative ring supplies the required commutative-semiring structure, so the intended ring case is included without restriction.

The target is an element of `AlgebraicCombinatorics.BivFPS ℚ`, whose body is `MvPowerSeries (Fin 2) ℚ`, matching the required `ℚ[[x,y]]`. Its coefficient function is exactly `fun nm => ↑((nm 0).choose (nm 1))`: for an exponent vector `nm`, index `0` is the exponent of the first variable `x` (as confirmed by `BivFPS.x := MvPowerSeries.X 0`), and index `1` is the exponent of the second variable `y`. Thus the coefficient of `x^n y^k` is the rational cast of `Nat.choose n k`, i.e. `\binom n k`, exactly as required by “whose coefficient at $x^n y^k$ is $\binom n k$.”

The blueprint defines the closed form as `1 / (1 - x(1+y)) ∈ ℚ[[x,y]]`. The target has type `AlgebraicCombinatorics.BivFPS ℚ`, whose body is `MvPowerSeries (Fin 2) ℚ`, and its body is `(1 - BivFPS.x * (1 + BivFPS.y)).invOfUnit 1`. Here `x` and `y` are respectively `MvPowerSeries.X 0` and `MvPowerSeries.X 1`, while `invOfUnit 1` constructs the inverse using the denominator’s unit constant coefficient `1`. Thus the formal definition denotes exactly the stated reciprocal in the bivariate rational formal power series ring.

The body `fun ... f nm => (PowerSeries.coeff (nm 0)) (f (nm 1))` makes the coefficient at the bidegree encoded by `nm` equal to the `nm 0`-th coefficient of `f (nm 1)`. Thus, with coordinate `0` as `x` and coordinate `1` as `y`, it exactly realizes the blueprint clause “whose coefficient at $x^n y^k$ is the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f_k$.” The codomain is `BivFPS R`, whose body is `MvPowerSeries (Fin 2) R`, matching a bivariate formal power series. The binder `[CommSemiring R]` is weaker than the blueprint’s commutative-ring setting, so the definition is strictly more general rather than weakened by an added hypothesis; in particular, it applies in the intended commutative-ring setting.

The coefficient formula is faithful: the body sets `m' := m + fun₀ | i => 1` and returns `↑(m' i) * (MvPowerSeries.coeff m') f`, which is exactly `(m_i + 1) · a_{m+e_i}`. The `LinearMap` result also matches “This defines an `R`-linear map,” and `[DecidableEq σ]` is an encoding requirement for constructing `e_i`, not a mathematical restriction. However, the elaborated signature adds `[inst : CommSemiring R]`, while the informal statement imposes no commutativity assumption on `R`; `R` appears only in `R[[x]]` and “an `R`-linear map.” Since `LinearMap` and `MvPowerSeries.coeff` require only a `Semiring R`, commutativity is a genuine narrowing of the coefficient structures. Generalizing the target binder from `[CommSemiring R]` to `[Semiring R]` (and adjusting the proofs accordingly) would remove the drift.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.ops.justification: Every target adds the binder `{R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R]`, whereas the blueprint only speaks of coefficients in `K` and nowhere requires multiplication in `K` to be commutative. This is a mathematically contentful restriction, not merely an encoding requirement. The coefficient formulas themselves match the blueprint: addition and subtraction are componentwise; `Finset.antidiagonal n` is exactly the pairs `(i,j)` with `i+j=n`; scalar multiplication gives `c * coeff n f`; and `PowerSeries.C a` has coefficient `a` at zero and zero otherwise. To remove the drift, weaken the coefficient assumption: `[Semiring R]` suffices for the addition, multiplication, constant, and scalar-multiplication formulas, while `[Ring R]` suffices for subtraction; alternatively, use `[Ring R]` uniformly. The informal statement would instead need to explicitly stipulate that `K` is a commutative ring to justify the current binders.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.par.justification: The target is exactly the integer formal power series whose coefficient at each natural index `n` is the partition number: `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(AlgebraicCombinatorics.partitionCount n)`. Its dependency unfolds as `partitionCount n = Fintype.card n.Partition`, and `Nat.Partition` is documented as the type of partitions of `n`, so this coefficient is the number `p(n)`, cast canonically from `ℕ` to `ℤ`. Thus it represents the blueprint’s `P = ∑_{n≥0} p(n) x^n ∈ ℤ[[x]]`. The formal restriction of coefficient indices to `ℕ` matches `n ≥ 0` in the displayed sum; the informal definition of `p(n)` for all integers does not require negative indices in this generating function.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.pol.justification: The body `fun {K} [CommRing K] f => {n | (PowerSeries.coeff n) f ≠ 0}.Finite` faithfully captures part (a): saying that the set of indices with nonzero coefficient is finite is equivalent to “all but finitely many coefficients of `a` are `0`.” The binders `{K} [CommRing K] f` also match the fixed commutative ring and an FPS over it. However, the informal statement also contains part (b): “We let `K[x]` be the set of all polynomials … This set `K[x]` is a subring of `K[[x]]`.” `FPS.IsPolynomial : PowerSeries K → Prop` neither defines this set/notion `K[x]` nor states its subring property. Thus it formalizes only part (a), not the full blueprint statement. To make the package faithful, either restrict the associated informal statement to part (a), or add a declaration defining `K[x]` from `FPS.IsPolynomial` and a declaration asserting/providing its subring structure.

The visible parts align: the target has `{K : Type u_1} → [CommRing K] → (f : PowerSeries K) → FPS.IsPolynomial f → Polynomial K`, while the blueprint fixes a commutative ring, assumes “$f\in K[[x]]$ [is] a polynomial FPS,” and produces an element of `$K[X]`. Moreover, `FPS.IsPolynomial f` is defined as `{n | PowerSeries.coeff n f ≠ 0}.Finite`, matching “all but finitely many coefficients … are $0$.” However, the decisive bound is hidden in the body `(fun N => (PowerSeries.trunc N) f) ⋯.choose`. The package does not give the proposition proved by `⋯`, nor the signature of Lemma `lem.fps.pol.degree-bound`, so it is impossible to verify that the chosen `N` is the degree bound required by “the truncation of $f$ at the degree bound given by Lemma …,” rather than an unrelated natural number. To decide faithfulness, the package must expose the existential proposition supplied to `Exists.choose` (and, if needed, the degree-bound lemma), showing that the chosen `N` bounds all nonzero coefficients in the sense expected by `PowerSeries.trunc`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.pow.justification: The defining formula is aligned: the body is `fpsExp (c • fpsLog f)`, matching `f^c := Exp(c Log f)`. However, the blueprint restricts the input and output: “Let `f ∈ K[[x]]₁`” and defines the result “`∈ K[[x]]₁`.” The elaborated signature instead has the unrestricted binder `f : PowerSeries K` and codomain `PowerSeries K`. Widening the input to a total extension is not itself a problem, but the raw codomain does not encode or assert the required constant-term-one result. The same erasure occurs in the dependencies: `fpsLog : PowerSeries K → PowerSeries K` rather than `K[[x]]₁ → K[[x]]₀`, and `fpsExp : PowerSeries K → PowerSeries K` rather than `K[[x]]₀ → K[[x]]₁`. To make the declaration faithful, introduce predicates or subtypes for constant term `0` and `1`, then give `fpsPow` an input in the constant-term-one subtype and an output in that subtype (with the corresponding proof); alternatively retain the total helper definitions but wrap them in a restricted `fpsPow` and prove its output has constant term `1`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.pro.justification: The body `(Function.support f).Finite`, together with `Function.support` meaning `{i | f i ≠ 0}`, says that only finitely many indices have nonzero values. This is exactly the informal condition that “all but finitely many i ∈ I satisfy k_i = 0.” The binders `{I : Type u_2} → {M : Type u_3} → [Zero M] → (I → M) → Prop` express the arbitrary indexed family in part (b), and part (a) is its specialization to the sequence index set. Allowing any value type `M` equipped only with zero is a harmless generalization of the unspecified values `k_i`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.sub.justification: All three declarations add the mathematically substantive binder `[inst : CommRing K]`: for example, `fps_comp` has `{K : Type u_1} → [inst : CommRing K] → ...`, and both coefficient theorems begin `∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K] ...`. The informal statement merely says “Let f and g be two FPSs in K[[x]]” and none of the supplied informal definitions states that `K` is a commutative ring. Under the package rules, that ambient assumption cannot be inferred from missing context. Thus the formal declarations only define and characterize composition for a restricted class of coefficient types, whereas the blueprint does not impose that restriction. The difference enters through the `CommRing K` requirement of the dependency `PowerSeries.subst`, which is inherited by all three targets. Apart from this restriction, the bodies and formulas match: `fun ... => PowerSeries.subst g f`, the hypothesis `PowerSeries.constantCoeff g = 0`, and `Finset.range (n + 1)` respectively represent substitution, `[x^0]g = 0`, and the range `d = 0,…,n`; the `finsum` formula is supported finitely under that hypothesis. To make the package faithful, either the blueprint must explicitly assume that `K` is a commutative ring, or `PowerSeries.subst` and these declarations must be generalized to the coefficient structure actually stipulated by the blueprint.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.sum.justification: The coefficientwise conditions and sum bodies match the blueprint: `∀ (n : ℕ), {i | (PowerSeries.coeff n) (f i) ≠ 0}.Finite` is exactly “for each n, all but finitely many i … satisfy [xⁿ]aᵢ = 0,” and `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ∑ᶠ i, (PowerSeries.coeff n) (f i)` gives the required essentially finite coefficient sum because the supplied `SummableFPS f` proves each support finite. However, both declarations add the binder `[CommRing R]`, while the informal statement does not restrict K to a commutative ring. This is mathematically contentful: the definition only uses coefficients, zero, and finite addition, and the available `PowerSeries.coeff` interface can already state it under `[Semiring R]`. Thus the formal declarations exclude, for example, noncommutative semirings without support from the blueprint. Change the `[CommRing R]` binder in both `SummableFPS` and `summableFPSSum` to `[Semiring R]` (or otherwise explicitly add the commutative-ring setting to the blueprint) to make them faithful.

The summability clause is represented exactly: the blueprint says “for each coefficient index n, only finitely many [x^n](f_i) are nonzero,” while `SummableFPS₀` has body `∀ (n : ℕ), {i | (PowerSeries.coeff n) ↑(f i) ≠ 0}.Finite`. Its sum is constructed coefficientwise by `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ∑ᶠ i, coeff n ↑(f i)` and returned as `PowerSeries₀`, matching both the blueprint’s essentially finite coefficientwise sum and the assertion that it belongs to `K⟦X⟧₀`. For products, `MultipliableFPS₁ f` is `PowerSeries.Multipliable fun i => ↑(f i)`, whose body is `∀ n, CoeffFinitelyDeterminedInProd ... n`, exactly the blueprint definition of multipliability. For members of `PowerSeries₁` (constant coefficient 1), this is equivalent to the helper characterization that outside a finite set all coefficients of `f_i - 1` in degrees `1 ≤ k ≤ n` vanish: adjoining one index at a time gives the forward implication degree-by-degree, and the finite union of exceptional sets gives finite determination in the reverse direction. `multipliableFPS₁Prod` constructs the blueprint-defined infinite product using `PowerSeries.tprod` and returns it in `PowerSeries₁`, matching the final membership assertion. The formal binders require only `[CommRing K]`, whereas the section convention assumes a commutative `ℚ`-algebra; this weaker hypothesis makes the declarations strictly more general, not weaker, so it is faithful.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.wco.justification: All five declarations match the corresponding clauses. (a) `WeakComposition := List ℕ` represents a finite ordered tuple whose entries are natural numbers, and `Nat` is “the natural numbers, starting at zero,” hence nonnegative integers. (b) `size α := List.sum α` is exactly the sum of the entries. (c) `len α := List.length α` is exactly the number of parts. (d) `ofSize n := { α // α.size = n }` is precisely the subtype of weak compositions having size `n`. (e) `ofSizeIntoParts n k := { α // α.size = n ∧ α.len = k }` is precisely the subtype having both size `n` and length `k`. The binders `n k : ℕ` agree with the blueprint’s `n,k ∈ ℕ`, and no additional hypotheses or restrictions are introduced.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.x.justification: Both declarations add the binder `[inst : CommRing R]`, while the blueprint only says that an FPS is a sequence of elements of `K` and characterizes `x` by coefficients `0` and `1`; it does not require additive inverses or commutative multiplication. Thus the formal statements cover only commutative rings. This restriction enters directly through both targets’ `[CommRing R]` binders and is stronger even than the `[Semiring R]` required by `PowerSeries.coeff` and `PowerSeries.X`. The coefficient conclusions themselves faithfully match the blueprint: `(PowerSeries.coeff 1) PowerSeries.X = 1` and, for every `i : ℕ` with `i ≠ 1`, `(PowerSeries.coeff i) PowerSeries.X = 0`. At minimum, replacing `[CommRing R]` by `[Semiring R]` would remove the unnecessary ring and commutativity assumptions imposed by the targets. To match the blueprint literally, the dependencies `PowerSeries.coeff` and `PowerSeries.X` would need versions requiring only enough structure to supply `0` and `1`, followed by correspondingly generalized target binders.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.xn-.justification: Both targets formalize part (b). `PowerSeries.CoeffFinitelyDeterminedInProd` has body `∃ M, PowerSeries.DeterminesCoeffInProd a M n`, exactly matching “there is a finite subset M of I that determines the xⁿ-coefficient in the product.” Here the inferred witness type is `Finset I`, representing a finite subset. The dependency expands to `∀ (J : Finset I), M ⊆ J → coeff n (∏ i ∈ J, a i) = coeff n (∏ i ∈ M, a i)`, matching the informal definition’s quantification over finite `J` with `M ⊆ J ⊆ I`; `J ⊆ I` is encoded by `J : Finset I`. `AlgebraicCombinatorics.FPS.CoeffFinitelyDetermined` is a direct alias of that predicate. The binders `[CommRing R]` and `[CommRing K]` supply the algebraic setting needed for the stated FPS operations and unordered finite products, rather than adding an unrelated hypothesis.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.xne.justification: The coefficient condition itself is exact: the body `∀ m ≤ n, (PowerSeries.coeff m) f = (PowerSeries.coeff m) g` matches “each m ∈ {0,1,…,n} satisfies [x^m]f = [x^m]g.” However, the elaborated signature adds the binder `[CommSemiring R]`, whereas the blueprint defines an FPS over `K` merely as a sequence in `K^ℕ` and places no commutative-semiring hypothesis on `K`. This is a mathematically contentful restriction unrelated to coefficient equality, so the formal relation has a narrower domain. The difference enters through `PowerSeries.XnEquiv`’s `[CommSemiring R]` binder, partly forced by the chosen `PowerSeries.coeff`, whose signature requires `[Semiring R]`; commutativity is unnecessary even for that dependency. To be faithful to the supplied blueprint, the declaration should quantify over an arbitrary coefficient type and use a coefficient projection available without algebraic structure (or that dependency should be generalized accordingly).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.gf-ws.d.justification: The blueprint defines the carrier as the tagged disjoint union “({0} × A) ∪ ({1} × B)” and requires each component’s weights to be inherited. The formal declaration takes arbitrary weighted sets, `{α : Type u_2} → {β : Type u_3} → WeightedSet α → WeightedSet β`, and returns `WeightedSet (α ⊕ β)`. By the documented meaning of `Sum`, `α ⊕ β` is exactly a tagged disjoint union. Its body sets `weight := Sum.elim W₁.weight W₂.weight`, so an `inl a` receives `W₁.weight a` and an `inr b` receives `W₂.weight b`, exactly matching the two displayed weight equations. There are no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.gf-ws.p.justification: The blueprint defines the carrier as the Cartesian product and requires “for any (a,b) ∈ A×B” that “|(a,b)| = |a| + |b|.” The elaborated signature takes arbitrary weighted sets `W₁ : WeightedSet α` and `W₂ : WeightedSet β` and returns `WeightedSet (α × β)`, so its carrier is exactly the product type. Its body sets `weight := fun (a, b) => W₁.weight a + W₂.weight b`, exactly matching the prescribed componentwise sum. There are no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.gf-ws.w.justification: Parts (a), (b), (d), and (e) match directly. `WeightedSet.mk : (α → ℕ) → WeightedSet α` represents “a set A equipped with a function w : A → ℕ”; `IsFiniteType` is `∀ (n : ℕ), {a | W.weight a = n}.Finite`, exactly “for each n ∈ ℕ, finitely many a have weight n.” `Isomorphism.mk` consists of `toEquiv : α ≃ β` and `∀ a, W₂.weight (toEquiv a) = W₁.weight a`, matching a weight-preserving bijection, while `AreIsomorphic := Nonempty (W₁.Isomorphism W₂)` propositionally expresses existence of such an isomorphism. For (c), `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(W.countOfWeight hft n)` has as its n-th coefficient the number of elements of weight n. The formal binder `{R : Type u_1} → [CommSemiring R]` generalizes the blueprint’s specific codomain `ℤ[[x]]` to power series over any commutative semiring via the natural-number cast; specializing to `R = ℤ` gives the stated generating function. This is a strictly more general definition, not a weakening or added restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.gf.weig.justification: The three definitions match the three blueprint clauses. For (a), the binders `(n : ℕ) → Even n → n ≥ 2` faithfully encode “each even positive integer n”: for an even natural number, positivity is equivalent to being at least 2. The body’s `basementDominos n`, `leftWall`, `rightWall n`, `middleDominos n`, and `topDominos n` have exactly the listed coordinates and ranges; the zero-based `Finset.range` indices are shifted so that they reproduce the blueprint’s indices `i ∈ [n/2]` and `i ∈ [n/2-1]`. For (b), `TilingB` has the same binders and its component definitions swap rows 1 and 3 while fixing row 2, exactly realizing “reflecting A_n across the horizontal axis.” For (c), `TilingC : DominoTiling 2 3` contains precisely the three horizontal dominos `{(1,1),(2,1)}`, `{(1,2),(2,2)}`, and `{(1,3),(2,3)}`. Finally, `DominoTiling` requires containment, full coverage, and pairwise disjointness, so each constructed object really is the asserted tiling.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.infsum..justification: The body correctly captures part (a): `EssentiallyFinite f` unfolds to `(Function.support f).Finite`, and `Function.support` is exactly `{i | f i ≠ 0}`, matching “the set `{ i ∈ I | a_i ≠ 0 }` is finite.” However, the target adds the mathematically substantive binder `[CommRing R]`, whereas this finiteness notion only needs a zero element; indeed the project dependency is stated with `[Zero M]`. Since the blueprint does not fix `K` to be a commutative ring, this narrows the families covered. The target should be generalized from `{R} → [CommRing R] → ...` to `{M} → [Zero M] → ...`. Moreover, the supplied informal statement also contains part (b), defining the infinite sum of an essentially finite family as the finite sum over its support, while the target is only a predicate `(ι → R) → Prop` and asserts no such definition or equality. Part (b) would require a separate infinite-sum declaration with the appropriate additive structure.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.isdbloc.justification: The body matches the blueprint clause by clause: `S ⊆ Finset.range n` expresses `S ⊆ {0, …, n-1}`; `∀ i < n / d` quantifies over block indices `{0, …, ⌊n/d⌋-1}` because natural-number division rounds down; and `(∀ j < d, i * d + j ∈ S) ∨ ∀ j < d, i * d + j ∉ S` says respectively that all or none of `{id, id+1, …, id+d-1}` lie in `S`. There are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.eva.justification: The target quantifies over unrestricted integer parameters, with signature `ℤ → ℤ → ℚ → ℚ → JacobiRing → PowerSeries ℚ`, while the blueprint requires each Laurent monomial to be replaced by `v^ℓ x^{ae+bℓ}` in `ℚ[[x]]`. The dependency `evalLaurentCoeffShifted` instead uses `PowerSeries.X ^ (a * ↑e + b * ℓ).toNat`; by the supplied definition of `Int.toNat`, every negative exponent is converted to `0`. Thus, for example, with `e = 0`, `b = 1`, and a coefficient containing `z⁻¹`, the blueprint asks for a term involving `x⁻¹`, which is not an element of `PowerSeries ℚ`, whereas Lean produces `X^0`. The difference enters through the body of `AlgebraicCombinatorics.evalLaurentCoeffShifted`, specifically the `.toNat` exponent. As stated for unrestricted `a`, `b`, and Laurent coefficients, the blueprint cannot be represented in the supplied `PowerSeries ℚ` codomain. It would require an integer-indexed Laurent/doubly-infinite-series codomain, which is not supplied as a project definition, or the blueprint and declaration would need explicit hypotheses guaranteeing `a·e+b·ℓ ≥ 0` for every contributing term (along with the needed coefficientwise summability condition).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.exc.justification: The target quantifies as required over every integer and partition: `ℤ → {n : ℕ} → n.Partition → AlgebraicCombinatorics.State`, matching “for any partition … and any ℓ ∈ ℤ,” with no added mathematical hypotheses. Its `levels` field is `excitedStateLevels ell mu`, whose body is `{p | p < ell - ↑k} ∪ {p | ∃ i, p = ell - 1 - ↑↑i + ↑(parts.get … i)}`, where the parts are sorted decreasingly. Under the declared convention that integer `p` represents the level `p + 1/2`, the informal level `ℓ - i + 1/2 + λ_i` for one-based `i ∈ {1,…,k}` is represented by the integer `ℓ - i + λ_i`; with formal zero-based index `i`, this is exactly `ell - 1 - i + parts[i]`. Likewise, represented levels below `ℓ-k` are exactly the integers satisfying `p < ell-k`. Sorting the multiset of partition parts decreasingly supplies the usual ordered tuple `(λ₁,…,λₖ)`. The two proof fields merely establish that this explicit set satisfies the informal definition of a state and impose no additional restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.fro.justification: The target quantifies over exactly two finite subsets via `Finset ℕ → Finset ℕ → AlgebraicCombinatorics.State`, matching “a pair `(P, N)` of finite subsets of `ℕ`.” Its level set is `{p | p ≥ 0 ∧ Int.toNat p ∈ P ∨ p < 0 ∧ Int.toNat (-p - 1) ∉ N}`, which matches `{p ≥ 0 : p ∈ P} ∪ {p < 0 : (-p-1) ∉ N}` under the project's stated representation of the half-integer level `p + 1/2` by `p : ℤ`. In the first branch `p ≥ 0`, and in the second branch `p < 0` makes `-p-1 ≥ 0`, so the uses of `Int.toNat` are precisely the coercions needed to test membership in `P, N : Finset ℕ`; no negative value is collapsed to zero in either guarded branch. The `State` constructor’s finiteness fields encode exactly the required state conditions and add no hypothesis on the inputs.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.gro.justification: The blueprint quantifies “For ℓ ∈ ℤ” and defines `G_ℓ := { all levels < ℓ }`. The target has signature `ℤ → AlgebraicCombinatorics.State` and body `fun ell => { levels := {p | p < ell}, ... }`. By the project definition, a level represented by `p : ℤ` denotes the half-integer `p + 1/2`; for integer `ell`, `p + 1/2 < ell` is equivalent to `p < ell`. Thus `{p | p < ell}` represents exactly all half-integer levels below ℓ. The `finite_nonneg` and `finite_negative_missing` fields merely establish that this set satisfies the blueprint’s definition of a state and add no hypothesis or restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.jac.justification: The target body `∏' (n : ℕ), AlgebraicCombinatorics.jacobiFactorQ n` ranges over naturals starting at zero, while `jacobiFactorQ` is defined by `fun n => 1 - PowerSeries.X ^ (2 * (n + 1))`. Thus its factors are exactly `(1-q^{2(n+1)})`, and reindexing by the positive integer `n+1` gives the blueprint’s `∏_{n>0}(1-q^{2n})`. The codomain is `JacobiRing`, whose body is `PowerSeries (LaurentPolynomial ℤ)`, matching `(ℤ[z^{±}])[[q]]`. Although Lean’s `tprod` is an unconditional topological product rather than the blueprint’s coefficient-stabilized definition, for this family the exponents tend upward, so each fixed coefficient is affected by only finitely many nontrivial factors; consequently the family is multipliable in the blueprint’s sense and the coefficientwise product agrees with the stated infinite FPS product. There are no additional binders or hypotheses restricting the blueprint statement.

The formal body `∏' (n : ℕ), jacobiFactorZ n * jacobiFactorZInv n` is the same product as the blueprint’s `∏_{n>0} ((1+q^{2n-1}z)(1+q^{2n-1}z^{-1}))`, after reindexing positive integers by `n ↦ n+1`. Indeed, the dependency bodies use exponent `2 * n + 1`, so at formal index `n = 0,1,…` they give the blueprint exponents `2(n+1)-1`. The factors use `jacobiZ = C (T 1)` and `jacobiZInv = C (T (-1))`, representing `z` and `z⁻¹`, and the result type `JacobiRing = PowerSeries (LaurentPolynomial ℤ)` is exactly `(ℤ[z^{±}])[[q]]`. The topology required by `tprod` is formal infrastructure for expressing the infinite product and introduces no additional mathematical hypothesis.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.jum.justification: The formal binders exactly encode the blueprint hypotheses: `S : State`, `p : Level`, `q : ℕ`, `p ∈ S.levels`, `p + ↑q ∉ S.levels`, and `q > 0` correspond to “If S is a state, p ∈ S, and q is a positive integer such that p+q ∉ S.” Since `Level` is defined as `ℤ`, casting `q : ℕ` into the level type correctly represents moving a positive integer number of steps. The body has `levels := S.levels \ {p} ∪ {p + ↑q}`, exactly matching `(S \ {p}) ∪ {p+q}`. The remaining constructor fields merely prove that this set is again a `State`, as the informal statement requires.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.par.justification: The body faithfully captures only the left-hand expression: `∑' (p : (n : ℕ) × n.Partition), PowerSeries.X ^ (2 * p.fst)` indexes all partitions `p` of `n` and contributes `q^(2n)` in `JacobiRing = PowerSeries (LaurentPolynomial ℤ)`. However, the informal statement also asserts the equality `∑ _{μ partition} q^{2|μ|} = ∏ _{k>0}(1-q^{2k})^{-1}`. The target is merely a definition with the sum as its body and contains no assertion of the product formula, so it does not imply the full blueprint statement. The difference enters in the target body, not through a binder or dependency. To make the formalization faithful, retain this definition and add a theorem identifying `partitionGenFunJacobi` with the indicated infinite product (supplying an appropriate formal-power-series infinite-product definition if needed).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.sig.justification: The body `PowerSeries.mk fun n => if n = 0 then 0 else ↑((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1) n)` defines an integer formal power series whose constant coefficient is zero and whose coefficient at every positive `n` is the integer cast of `σ 1 n`. The library specifies that `ArithmeticFunction.sigma` gives the sum of the `k`th powers of the divisors, so `sigma 1 n` is exactly `∑_{d ∣ n} d`. Thus this matches `S = ∑_{k>0} σ(k) x^k ∈ ℤ[[x]]`, including the absence of a constant term.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.jtp.sta.justification: The `State` constructor faithfully captures the state condition: `levels : Set AlgebraicCombinatorics.Level`, `{p | p ≥ 0 ∧ p ∈ levels}.Finite`, and `{p | p < 0 ∧ p ∉ levels}.Finite` exactly encode, under `Level = ℤ` representing `p + 1/2`, “only finitely many positive levels” and “all but finitely many negative levels.” However, the informal statement also says, “For any state S, we define” both `energy S ... ∈ ℕ` and `parnum S ... ∈ ℤ`. The target body contains only `State.mk` and provides neither definition. Thus it formalizes only the first part of the blueprint. To make the whole statement faithful, retain this `State` declaration and add definitions `energy : State → ℕ` and `parnum : State → ℤ` implementing the displayed sums and cardinality difference, with the half-integer representation accounted for.

The blueprint sums over “all integer–partition pairs $(\ell,\mu)$” with monomial $q^{\ell^2+2|\mu|}z^\ell$. The target indexes `∑' (pair : ℤ × (n : ℕ) × n.Partition)`, equivalently an integer together with a dependent pair of `n : ℕ` and `μ : n.Partition`. Thus `n` is exactly `|μ|`, and every partition contributes once, even though the partition value itself does not occur in the summand. Its summand is `stateMonomial (ℓ.natAbs ^ 2 + 2 * n) ℓ`, whose body is `PowerSeries.X ^ e * jacobiZPow p`, while `jacobiZPow ℓ` is the constant power series containing `LaurentPolynomial.T ℓ`; hence this is precisely $q^{\ell^2+2|\mu|}z^\ell$. Using `ℓ.natAbs ^ 2 : ℕ` faithfully represents the nonnegative exponent $\ell^2$. The codomain `JacobiRing` is definitionally `PowerSeries (LaurentPolynomial ℤ)`, matching $(\mathbb Z[z^{\pm1}])[[q]]`. Finally, `tsum` supplies the unconditional sum in the pointwise topology on power series; here each $q$-coefficient receives contributions from only finitely many such indexed pairs, so it agrees with the blueprint’s coefficientwise formal sum.

The target has binders `ℕ → ℤ → AlgebraicCombinatorics.JacobiRing`, matching a natural-number energy exponent `e` for the FPS variable and an integer particle-number exponent `p`, as required by the Laurent variable `z`. Its body `fun e p => PowerSeries.X ^ e * AlgebraicCombinatorics.jacobiZPow p` is exactly `q^e z^p`: `PowerSeries.X` is the formal-power-series variable (called `q` by the blueprint convention), while `jacobiZPow p` is defined as the constant power series `PowerSeries.C (LaurentPolynomial.T p)`, and `LaurentPolynomial.T p` denotes `z^p`. Finally, `JacobiRing` is definitionally `PowerSeries (LaurentPolynomial ℤ)`, i.e. `(ℤ[z^{±}])[[q]]`, exactly the ambient ring stated informally.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.kron-de.justification: The body `if i = j then 1 else 0` exactly matches “δᵢⱼ = 1 if i = j; 0 if i ≠ j,” with the result in `K`. The binder `[CommRing K]` matches the section convention fixing a commutative ring `K`. The binder `[DecidableEq α]` is only the computational evidence required by `ite` to decide `i = j`, so it encodes the piecewise definition rather than adding a mathematically substantive hypothesis. Quantifying `{K}` and `{α}` makes the definition at least as general as the blueprint’s fixed `K` and ‘any objects.’

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.ksubset.justification: The target defines `kSubsets n k` as `Finset.powersetCard k (Finset.range n)`. By the cited library definitions, `Finset.range n` is exactly the set of naturals less than `n`, i.e. `{0, …, n-1}`, and `Finset.powersetCard k` returns exactly its subsets of cardinality `k`. Thus it matches `\{S \subseteq \{0,\ldots,n-1\} : |S|=k\}` with the same natural-number parameters `n` and `k`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.lgv.cro.justification: All four definitions match the corresponding clauses. For (a), `isCrowded` is `∃ i j, i ≠ j ∧ v ∈ pt.verticesOf i ∧ v ∈ pt.verticesOf j`, exactly expressing that `v` lies on two distinct paths. For (b), `crowdedPathIndices` contains precisely those `i` for which `∃ j, i ≠ j ∧ ¬ Disjoint (pt.verticesOf i) (pt.verticesOf j)`; for sets of vertices, this says path `i` shares a vertex with another distinct path. For (c), `minCrowdedPathIndex` has the binder `(pt : LGV1.PathTuple k A B) → pt.isIntersecting → Fin k` and body `pt.crowdedPathIndices.min' ⋯`, matching “For an ipat … the smallest i in the crowded path indices”; `isIntersecting` is defined as the negation of pairwise disjointness, ensuring the crowded-index finset is nonempty. For (d), `crowdedVerticesOnPath pt i` is `{v | v ∈ pt.verticesOf i ∧ ∃ j, i ≠ j ∧ v ∈ pt.verticesOf j}`, exactly the vertices on path `i` appearing on another path. The use of `Fin k` is the standard finite indexing encoding, and its zero-based representation preserves the ordering needed for the minimum.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.lgv.lat.justification: The formal definitions exactly specify the blueprint’s graph. `LatticePoint` has body `ℤ × ℤ`, matching “vertex set ℤ²,” and `IntegerLatticeAdj` has body `q = (p.1 + 1, p.2) ∨ q = (p.1, p.2 + 1)`, matching exactly the two stated arc forms and excluding all others. `integerLattice` installs precisely this relation as the `Digraph` adjacency. The two constructors `LatticeStep.east` and `LatticeStep.north` match the two kinds of steps. The graph is simple: adjacency is relational, so there are no parallel arcs, and neither listed successor equals its source over ℤ. The final path-determinacy observation follows from each east or north step having a uniquely determined successor from any starting point. There are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.lgv.pat.justification: All five declarations match the corresponding clauses. (a) `LGV1.kVertex k = Fin k → LGV1.LatticePoint` represents a `k`-tuple of lattice points, with `LatticePoint = ℤ × ℤ`. (b) `fun v σ i => v (σ i)` gives the tuple whose `i`th entry is `A_{σ(i)}`, exactly as in “(A_{σ(1)},…,A_{σ(k)})”; using `Fin k` is the standard zero-based encoding of the finite index set. (c) `PathTuple.mk` stores `paths : Fin k → LatticePath` together with `∀ i, (paths i).isPathFromTo (A i) (B i)`, while `isPathFromTo` means `path.endpoint a = b`, so each component is a path from `A_i` to `B_i`. The path representation uses precisely the east and north steps fixed by the lattice definition. (d) `∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (pt.verticesOf i) (pt.verticesOf j)` says every pair of distinct paths has disjoint vertex sets, matching “no two ... have any vertex in common.” Here `verticesOf` uses `LatticePath.vertices`, whose body lists the starting point and all successive points, including the endpoint. (e) `fun pt => ¬ pt.isNonIntersecting` exactly formalizes “intersecting if it is not non-intersecting.” There are no added hypotheses or mathematically contentful restrictions.

All three declarations match the three blueprint clauses without added hypotheses. For (a), `pathMatrixK : {k : ℕ} → kVertex k → kVertex k → Matrix (Fin k) (Fin k) ℤ` has body `Matrix.of fun i j => ↑(numPaths (A i) (B j))`, exactly giving the `k × k` integer matrix with entry `# paths(A_i → B_j)`. For (b), `numNipatsK` has body `(nipatsFromTo A (B.permute σ)).ncard`; `B.permute σ i = B (σ i)` agrees with the informal `σ(B) = (B_{σ(1)},…,B_{σ(k)})`, and `nipatsFromTo` selects precisely path tuples whose distinct paths have disjoint vertex sets. For (c), `numIpatsK` analogously uses `(ipatsFromTo A (B.permute σ)).ncard`, where `isIntersecting` is defined as `¬ isNonIntersecting`, matching the blueprint. The use of `Fin k` is the standard zero-based encoding of the blueprint index set `[k]`, and the natural path counts are cast to `ℤ` for the required integer matrix.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.lgv.sig.justification: The declarations match all three clauses for arbitrary lattice points, with no added hypotheses: each signature quantifies only `{A A' B B' : LGV1.LatticePoint}` or takes four such points. For (a), `SignedPathTuple2.mk` stores `(path0 path1 : LGV1.LatticePath)` and `(toBB' : Bool)`, with endpoint proofs sending them to `(B,B')` when true and `(B',B)` when false; `sign` is correspondingly `if spt.toBB' = true then 1 else -1`, exactly the stated signs. For (b), `pathMatrix2 A A' B B'` is `!![↑(numPaths A B), ↑(numPaths A B'); ↑(numPaths A' B), ↑(numPaths A' B')]`, the required 2×2 integer path-count matrix. For (c), `numNipats2` forms the two-vertices `![A,A']` and `![B,B']` and takes `(nipatsFromTo AB BB).ncard`; `nipatsFromTo` is defined by `pt.isNonIntersecting`, whose body requires distinct paths to have disjoint vertex sets, matching the blueprint definition of nipats. The auxiliary `isIntersecting` uses `∃ v ∈ spt.path0.vertices A, v ∈ spt.path1.vertices A'`, which for two paths matches having a common vertex.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.fl.justification: The decisive declarations are `FloorCeiling.floor_def`, with `∀ (a : ℝ) (n : ℤ), n ≤ ⌊a⌋ ↔ ↑n ≤ a`, and `FloorCeiling.ceil_def`, with `∀ (a : ℝ) (n : ℤ), ⌈a⌉ ≤ n ↔ a ≤ ↑n`. Since `⌊a⌋` and `⌈a⌉` are integers, these characterize them respectively as the greatest integer at most `a` and the least integer at least `a`, exactly matching the blueprint. The binders quantify over every real `a` and every integer `n`, with no added hypotheses. `floor_of_int`, `ceil_of_int`, and `nat_div_eq_floor` are ancillary consequences/applications; they do not weaken the two exact characterizations.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.ge.justification: The blueprint defines both series in `ℤ[[x]]`. The targets have type `PowerSeries ℤ`, which is precisely a formal power series over the integers. For `P`, the body `Nat.Partition.genFun fun x x_1 => 1` uses the documented partition generating function, whose coefficient at each `n` sums the character over all partitions of `n`; the constant character `1` therefore gives the number `p(n)`, matching `P := ∑_{n≥0} p(n) x^n`. For `S`, the body `PowerSeries.mk fun n => if n = 0 then 0 else ↑(Nat.Partition.divisorSum n)` gives constant coefficient zero and coefficient `σ(n)` for every positive `n`. The dependency `divisorSum n := (ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1) n`, together with the library meaning that `sigma 1` sums first powers of divisors, matches `σ(k) = ∑_{d∣k} d`. Thus it is exactly `S := ∑_{k≥1} σ(k)x^k`, with coefficients cast canonically from `ℕ` to `ℤ`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.iv.justification: The definition body `fun P ... => if P then 1 else 0` exactly implements the blueprint’s cases “1, if A is true; 0, if A is false.” The accompanying theorems state these two branches explicitly: `P → IversonBracket.iverson P = 1` and `¬P → IversonBracket.iverson P = 0`. Although the blueprint calls the result an integer, the formal binders `{α : Type u_1} [Zero α] [One α]` are a strictly more general codomain supporting designated `0` and `1`; they include the intended integer-valued interpretation rather than weakening it. The `[Decidable P]` binder is the formal computational setting required by `if P then 1 else 0`, not a substantive change to the truth-value cases. Finally, `∀ ... (i j : α), (if i = j then 1 else 0) = IversonBracket.iverson (i = j)` is precisely the stated identity `δ_{i,j} = [i=j]`, with the conditional representing the Kronecker delta. `[DecidableEq α]` supplies the decidability needed to evaluate that conditional and is an encoding requirement.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.od.justification: The informal statement quantifies over integers: “Let $n\in\mathbb Z$,” and defines both kinds of partitions and both counting functions for such $n$. All four Lean declarations restrict the index to naturals: `IsDistinctParts : {n : ℕ} → n.Partition → Prop`, `IsOddParts : {n : ℕ} → n.Partition → Prop`, and both counts have type `ℕ → ℕ`. This is a narrowed domain and leaves the definitions for negative integers unspecified, so it is weaker than the blueprint. On natural indices, the bodies are faithful: `p.parts.Nodup` means no repeated parts; `∀ i ∈ p.parts, Odd i` means every part is odd; and the cardinalities of `Nat.Partition.distincts n` and `Nat.Partition.odds n` give the stated counts. To make the package faithful, either the blueprint must say `n ∈ ℕ`, or the formal declarations must use an integer-indexed notion of partition/count, with no partitions—and hence count zero—for negative indices.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.pa.justification: The blueprint explicitly quantifies clause (c) over integers: “Let $n\in\mathbb Z$. A partition of $n$ means…”, whereas every relevant formal declaration is restricted by `{n : ℕ}`, through the dependency `Nat.Partition : ℕ → Type`; for example, `size_eq` has `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), p.parts.sum = n`, and `ofList'` likewise constructs only `n.Partition` for `n : ℕ`. This is a narrowed index range. The multiset representation itself is compatible with weakly decreasing tuples—each finite multiset of positive naturals has a canonical decreasing enumeration—and `0 < i` plus the sum equation correctly encode positivity and size. However, the formal declarations cannot even state the blueprint’s notion of a partition indexed by a negative integer (which should have no inhabitants). To make the formalization faithful, replace or wrap `Nat.Partition` with a type indexed by `ℤ`, with parts summing to the integer index (and hence empty for negative indices), or change the blueprint’s binder from `n ∈ ℤ` to `n ∈ ℕ`.

The first definition has signature `ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℕ` and body `fun k ℓ n => {p | p.numParts = k ∧ p.largestPart = ℓ}.card`, exactly matching `q_{k,ℓ}(n) := |{ p ⊢ n : ℓ(p) = k, largest part of p = ℓ }|`. Here `p : n.Partition`, `numParts` is `p.parts.card`, and `largestPart` is the maximum of the parts with value `0` for the empty partition, matching the supplied informal definitions. The total definition has signature `ℕ → ℕ → ℕ` and body `fun k ℓ => ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc k (k * ℓ), Nat.Partition.partsAndLargestCount k ℓ n`; since `Finset.Icc k (k * ℓ)` is the inclusive interval `k ≤ n ≤ kℓ`, this is exactly `Q(k,ℓ) := ∑_{n=k}^{kℓ} q_{k,ℓ}(n)`. There are no added mathematical hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.pe.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “any $k\in\mathbb Z$” and defines “$w_k\in\mathbb N$” by $((3k-1)k)/2$. The Lean signature `ℤ → ℕ` has exactly that domain and codomain, and its body is `fun k => ((3 * k - 1) * k / 2).toNat`. Here the arithmetic and division occur in `ℤ`. For every integer `k`, `(3k-1)k` is even and nonnegative (for `k ≤ 0`, both factors are nonpositive; for `k ≥ 1`, both are nonnegative), so integer division by `2` gives the exact nonnegative quotient. Consequently, `Int.toNat` does not truncate or alter the value. Thus the formal definition agrees with the stated natural-valued formula for every integer `k`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.pn.justification: The blueprint quantifies over integers: “Let n ∈ ℤ and k ∈ ℕ” in (a), and “Let n ∈ ℤ” in (b). The corresponding formal declarations restrict the index to naturals: `Nat.Partition.partsCount : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ` with body `fun k n => ...`, and `Nat.Partition.partitionCount : ℕ → ℕ` with body `fun n => ...`. Thus they do not define `p_k(n)` or `p(n)` for negative integers, even though the blueprint does; this narrowed domain is mathematically contentful drift. On nonnegative inputs, the bodies correctly count partitions with `p.parts.card = k` and all partitions, respectively. To make the declarations faithful, change the `n` binder in both definitions to `ℤ` (retaining `k : ℕ`) and define the count as zero for negative `n`, while using the existing `Nat.Partition` counts for nonnegative `n` (or introduce an integer-indexed partition type with no inhabitants at negative indices). `partsInCount` and `partsLeqCount` are auxiliary definitions not specified by this informal statement and do not repair the domain mismatch.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.qb.justification: The blueprint quantifies “Let n ∈ ℕ and k ∈ ℤ,” but the target’s corresponding binders are `ℕ → ℕ → R → R`: both `n` and `k` are restricted to naturals. Thus the formal definition has no cases for negative integer `k`, whereas the blueprint defines the coefficient for every integer `k` (with the partition sum empty, hence zero, outside the valid range). This difference enters at the target’s second numeric binder. A faithful version should take `k : ℤ`, return zero unless `0 ≤ k` and `k ≤ n`, and use `k.toNat` in `monotoneFunctions` in the remaining case. In addition, part (b) says “any element of a ring A,” while the target requires `[CommSemiring R]`; commutativity is an extra algebraic restriction not stated by the blueprint and excludes noncommutative rings. Since the body only uses finite sums, zero, and natural powers, `[Semiring R]` would cover arbitrary rings while remaining more general. For natural `0 ≤ k ≤ n`, the monotone tuples in `monotoneFunctions k (n-k)` correctly encode partitions with largest part at most `n-k` and length at most `k` by padding with zeros and reversing order.

The blueprint explicitly says in (c), “if a is an element of a ring A,” where the supplied definition of `ring` allows noncommutative multiplication. Both Lean declarations instead require the binder `[CommSemiring R]`. Thus `qInt` and `qFactorial` cannot be instantiated for a general noncommutative ring `A`; this is a mathematically substantive commutativity restriction, not merely encoding. The lack of additive inverses is harmless extra generality, but it does not compensate for excluding noncommutative rings. The restriction enters directly through `[CommSemiring R]` in both elaborated signatures and, for `qFactorial`, through `Finset.prod`, which requires a `CommMonoid`. To make the definitions faithful, `qInt` could use `[Semiring R]` (or `[Ring R]`), while `qFactorial` should use the same noncommutative-capable structure and replace the unordered `Finset.prod` with an ordered product/fold representing exactly `[1]ₐ[2]ₐ⋯[n]ₐ`. Generalizing from rings to semirings would then be acceptable stronger generality.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.re.justification: The two declarations exactly implement the two directions of the blueprint. For removal, the binder `{n : ℕ} → (p : n.Partition) → 1 ∈ p.parts` matches “a partition of n that contains 1 as a part,” and the result `(n - 1).Partition` matches “yields a partition of n−1.” Its body uses `p.parts.erase 1`, and `Multiset.erase` “subtracts 1 from the multiplicity,” so precisely one copy is removed. For addition, `{n : ℕ} → n.Partition → (n + 1).Partition` matches the converse, and the body uses `1 ::ₘ p.parts`, which adds exactly one occurrence of 1. Although natural subtraction saturates at zero, the removal hypothesis together with `Nat.Partition` being a multiset of positive integers summing to `n` ensures the relevant case has `n ≥ 1`. The use of `ℕ` does not lose realizable integer partitions here, since a finite tuple of positive integers cannot have negative size.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.su.justification: The two definitions implement exactly the two constructions in the blueprint. For subtraction, the binders `(p : n.Partition) → p.parts.card = k → (∀ x ∈ p.parts, x > 1) → (n - k).Partition` match “a partition of n into k parts with all parts > 1,” and the body maps every part by `fun x => x - 1`. Since every part is greater than 1, no mapped part is zero, so `Nat.Partition.ofSums`, which only removes zeros, preserves the `k` parts. For addition, `(p : n.Partition) → p.parts.card = k → (n + k).Partition` and `Multiset.map (fun x => x + 1) p.parts` match “adding 1 to each part of a partition of n into k parts”; mapped parts remain positive and retain cardinality `k`. Natural-number subtraction is not a mismatch here because the hypothesis that all `k` positive parts exceed 1 ensures the relevant total satisfies `n ≥ k`, so saturation at zero does not alter `n-k`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.partner.justification: The blueprint defines the partner of every “finite set $I$ of natural numbers” as “$I' := I \bigtriangleup \{0\}$.” The target has exactly the corresponding type and body: `Finset ℕ → Finset ℕ` and `fun I => symmDiff I {0}`. Here `Finset ℕ` represents finite sets of natural numbers, `{0}` is the singleton finset containing natural-number zero, and `symmDiff` is symmetric difference. By its supplied definition `(I \ {0}) ⊔ ({0} \ I)`, this removes `0` when `0 ∈ I` and adds it when `0 ∉ I`, matching both explanatory cases. The `DecidableEq ℕ`, lattice, and set-difference instances are inferred implementation machinery and impose no additional mathematical hypothesis.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pascal.justification: The three bodies exactly implement the blueprint formulas with 0-based indices. `pascalMatrix` has binders `(n : ℕ)` and `i j : Fin n`, so `↑i, ↑j` range over `0,…,n-1`, and its body `(↑i + ↑j).choose ↑i` is `A_{i,j} = \binom{i+j}{i}`. Likewise, `pascalLowerTriangular` uses `(↑i).choose ↑k`, matching `L_{i,k} = \binom{i}{k}`, and `pascalUpperTriangular` uses `(↑j).choose ↑k`, matching `U_{k,j} = \binom{j}{k}`. `Nat.choose` denotes the relevant binomial coefficient on these natural-number arguments, and the `Fin n` row and column types precisely encode the stated bounds `0 ≤ i,j,k ≤ n-1`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pent.co.justification: The target has exactly the required domain and codomain, `ℕ → ℤ`, and its body returns `(-1) ^ k.natAbs` when `pentagonalNumberInverse n = some k`, and `0` when it returns `none`, matching “`(-1)^{|k|}` if `n = w_k` for some `k ∈ ℤ`, `0` otherwise.” The dependency `pentagonalNumber` implements `w_k = ((3*k - 1)*k/2).toNat`; the product is always even and its quotient is nonnegative, so this agrees with the informal definition. The inverse searches positive indices `k = 0,…,n` and negative indices `-k-1` for `k = 0,…,n`. This range is exhaustive: for positive indices, `w_k ≥ k`, and for a negative index `-m`, `w_{-m} ≥ m`, so any index producing `n` lies in the searched range. Thus `none` occurs exactly when no such integer index exists, and the declaration faithfully implements the blueprint definition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pent.eu.justification: The blueprint defines “the infinite product \(\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}(1-x^k)\in R[[x]]\)” but does not require that the coefficient ring be commutative. Its FPS operations use addition, subtraction, multiplication, zero, and one, which support a ring setting, but none of the supplied informal definitions imposes commutativity. The elaborated target narrows the coefficient domain with the contentful binder `[CommRing R]`. Thus it only defines the Euler product for commutative rings, an added stronger typeclass hypothesis. The indexing itself is correct: `∏' (k : ℕ), (1 - PowerSeries.X ^ (k + 1))` reindexes \(k=1,2,\ldots\), and the discrete topology on `R` inducing the Pi topology on `PowerSeries R` matches the coefficientwise multipliable product. To be faithful, the `[CommRing R]` restriction should be weakened to the ring assumptions actually needed by the blueprint, with the product construction generalized if Mathlib’s unconditional `tprod`—which requires a `CommMonoid`—cannot directly support that weaker setting; alternatively, the blueprint would need to state that `R` is a commutative ring.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pent.pe.justification: The body matches the displayed coefficients: `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(pentagonalCoeff n)` defines the series coefficientwise, and `pentagonalCoeff` returns `(-1) ^ k.natAbs` when the inverse finds `n = w_k`, otherwise `0`, agreeing with the informal definition using `(-1)^{|k|}`. The finite inverse search also covers the relevant indices. However, the elaborated target has the contentful binder `{R : Type u_1} → [CommRing R] → PowerSeries R`, while the blueprint only says the series lies in `R[[x]]` and nowhere assumes that `R` is commutative. Thus the formal definition is restricted to commutative rings by an assumption absent from the blueprint. To make it faithful, either state in the blueprint that `R` is a commutative ring, or weaken the target binder to the intended coefficient structure—e.g. `AddGroupWithOne R` (which supplies the canonical integer cast), or another explicitly intended weaker class.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.ca.justification: The body `fun {n} σ => (List.map σ.lehmerBlock (List.finRange n)).flatten` exactly implements the blueprint formula `w(σ) = a₀ ++ a₁ ++ ⋯ ++ aₙ₋₁`: `List.finRange n` lists the indices `0, …, n-1` in order, `List.map σ.lehmerBlock` replaces each index by its Lehmer block, and `List.flatten` concatenates those blocks in that order. The elaborated signature `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Equiv.Perm.Word n` introduces no additional mathematical hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.cy.justification: The blueprint assumes “i₁, i₂, …, iₖ [are] k distinct elements,” which is represented by `l.Nodup` in `cyc_apply_getElem`. Its conclusion, `(cyc l) l[j] = l[(j + 1) % l.length]` for `j < l.length`, is exactly the zero-based version of sending each `i_j` to `i_{j+1}`, with reduction modulo `l.length` implementing `i_{k+1} = i₁`. The other case is supplied by `cyc_apply_of_not_mem`: `x ∉ l → (cyc l) x = x`, matching “leaves all other elements of X unchanged.” Finally, `cyc l : Equiv.Perm X` has the blueprint meaning of a permutation as a bijection `X → X`. Although the definition `cyc` accepts lists without `Nodup`, this is a harmless extension beyond the blueprint’s domain; the claimed behavior on distinct entries is stated under `l.Nodup`. The binder `[DecidableEq X]` is a constructive implementation requirement needed by `List.formPerm`, rather than a mathematical alteration of the cycle characterization.

Part (a) directly contradicts the blueprint. The informal statement explicitly says: “This includes 1-cycles, if there are any in the DCD of σ.” But `cycles` has body `σ.cycleFactorsFinset`, and its target docstring states: “This only includes cycles of length ≥ 2 (non-trivial cycles). Fixed points (1-cycles) are not included.” Thus the difference enters through `AlgebraicCombinatorics.CycleDecomposition.cycles`, specifically its use of `Equiv.Perm.cycleFactorsFinset`. It would need to include a separately represented 1-cycle for every fixed point. Merely adding the identity permutation is insufficient when there are multiple fixed points, since all singleton cycles induce the same permutation and a `Finset (Equiv.Perm α)` cannot distinguish them; consequently the codomain should represent cycles by their supports/orbits (or another representation retaining the fixed point), rather than only by permutations. The binders `[DecidableEq α]` and `[Fintype α]` are encoding requirements consistent with “Let X be a finite set,” not substantive drift. Part (b), `cycleLengthsPartition σ := σ.partition`, has the required type `(Fintype.card α).Partition`, but this does not repair the explicit mismatch in part (a); moreover the supplied base-library description “The partition corresponding to a permutation” does not independently specify how its parts are obtained.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.ev.justification: The bodies exactly match the blueprint’s defining conditions: `Equiv.Perm.IsEven σ` is `Equiv.Perm.sign σ = 1`, corresponding to “even if $(-1)^σ = 1$,” and `Equiv.Perm.IsOdd σ` is `Equiv.Perm.sign σ = -1`, corresponding to “odd if $(-1)^σ = -1$.” The library specifies that `Equiv.Perm.sign` returns `1` for even permutations and `-1` for odd permutations. The binders `{α : Type} [Fintype α] ... σ : Equiv.Perm α` are more general than the blueprint’s `n ∈ ℕ` and `σ ∈ S_n`: taking `α = Fin n` recovers `S_n`, while arbitrary finite `α` merely allows any finite underlying set. `[DecidableEq α]` is computational evidence needed by this sign construction, not a mathematically substantive restriction on finite sets.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.in.justification: The formal body `fun {n} σ i j => j < σ i ∧ i < σ⁻¹ j` exactly matches the informal definition: “A cell `(i, j)` is in the Rothe diagram of `σ` if `j < σ(i)` and `i < σ⁻¹(j)`.” The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Fin n → Fin n → Prop` encode the finite permutation setting and cell indices without adding any mathematically substantive hypothesis. The final sentence about cells not hit by the row or column of a permutation-matrix entry is explanatory rather than an additional condition.

The blueprint asks for “the explicit bijection between inversions of σ and inversions of σ⁻¹, sending (i,j) to (σ(j), σ(i)).” The target has exactly the type `{n : ℕ} → (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) → ↥σ.inversions ≃ ↥σ⁻¹.inversions`, and its underlying function applies `inversionBijAux σ`, whose body is `fun ... p => (σ p.2, σ p.1)`. Moreover, `Equiv.Perm.inversions` is defined by `p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.2 < σ p.1`, exactly matching the informal condition `i < j` and `σ(i) > σ(j)`. Using `Fin n` rather than `{1,…,n}` is the standard order-preserving finite-type encoding and does not add a mathematically contentful restriction. There are no additional hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The formal definition `fun {X} σ => σ * σ = 1` matches the blueprint condition `f ∘ f = id` under the stated permutation convention that multiplication is composition and `1` is the identity. This match is also made explicit by `IsInvolution σ ↔ Function.Involutive ⇑σ` and `IsInvolution σ ↔ ∀ (x : X), σ (σ x) = x`. The theorem `IsInvolution σ ↔ σ⁻¹ = σ` faithfully formalizes “equals its own inverse”; the reversed order of equality is immaterial. Although the binder is `{σ : Equiv.Perm X}` rather than an arbitrary function `f : X → X`, the blueprint itself states that every function satisfying the involution equation is automatically a permutation, so representing involutions directly as permutations imposes no mathematically contentful restriction. Using `X : Type u_1` for a set is also a standard encoding.

The blueprint quantifies over “n ∈ ℕ and σ ∈ S_n” and defines inversions by “i < j and σ(i) > σ(j).” The formal binder `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` represents a permutation of an n-element ordered set, and the body `{p | p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.1 > σ p.2}` selects exactly those ordered pairs satisfying the blueprint condition. Although `Fin n` is zero-based whereas the blueprint’s `[n]` is `{1,…,n}`, the order-preserving shift identifies these sets; this is an encoding choice, not a mathematical restriction. The second body `(AlgebraicCombinatorics.Perm.inv σ).card` is exactly the “# of inversions” required for the Coxeter length. No additional hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers are introduced.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.is.justification: The formal declaration says, for `{n : ℕ}` and `w : Equiv.Perm.Word n`, that `List.length w = (Equiv.Perm.wordProd w).length`, where `Equiv.Perm.length` is defined as `σ.inversions.card`. The blueprint says that the word is reduced when “its length `q` equals `ℓ(s_{k_1} ⋯ s_{k_q})`,” but the package supplies no informal definition of the notation `ℓ`. Thus it is not determined whether blueprint `ℓ` means inversion cardinality, Coxeter/minimal word length, or something else. The word and product definitions otherwise align: `Word n = List (Fin (n - 1))` and `wordProd` multiplies the corresponding simple transpositions in the stated order. To decide faithfulness, the package would need an INFORMAL DEFINITION fixing `ℓ`; if it defines `ℓ(σ)` as the number of inversions of `σ` (or an equivalent notion), the declaration is faithful.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.la.justification: The body `fun {n} σ i => {j | j < i ∧ σ j > σ i}.card` exactly implements the blueprint’s `g(σ,i) = |{ j < i : σ(j) > σ(i) }|`: `Finset.card` gives the cardinality, and the filtered universal finset ranges over all `j : Fin n`. The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Fin n → ℕ` encode `σ ∈ S_n` and `i ∈ [n]`. Although `Fin n` is zero-based while the blueprint defines `[n] = {1,…,n}`, the order-preserving shift between these sets preserves both inequalities and cardinality, so this is an encoding choice rather than mathematical drift. Negative integers from the general definition of `[n]` introduce no missing `(σ,i)` inputs because `[n]` is empty when `n < 0`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.le.justification: The dependency defines `lexLt a b` as `∃ k, (∀ i < k, a i = b i) ∧ a k < b k`, matching the blueprint’s condition that the first index where the tuples differ satisfies `a_k < b_k`: equality at every earlier index makes `k` the first possible difference, and `a k < b k` entails `a k ≠ b k`. Using `Fin n` is the standard zero-based encoding of the blueprint’s `n` positions `[n]` and does not change the lexicographic relation. The targets establish the required strict-total-order properties without added hypotheses: irreflexivity (`∀ ... a, ¬ lexLt a a`), transitivity, asymmetry, and exhaustive exclusive trichotomy for every `a b : Fin n → ℤ`. In particular, `lexLt_strictTotalOrder` explicitly states the three mutually exclusive cases `a = b`, `lexLt a b`, and `lexLt b a`, which is exactly the blueprint’s claim that `<_lex` is a strict total order on `ℤ^n`.

Expanding the formal conclusion `lehmerCode σ ∈ lehmerCodeSet n` gives `∀ i : Fin n, lehmerEntry σ i ≤ n - 1 - ↑i`. The entry is exactly `{j | i < j ∧ σ i > σ j}.card`, matching the blueprint’s count of positions to the right with smaller values. Lean uses zero-based `Fin n`; under the order-preserving correspondence between formal index `i : Fin n` and the blueprint’s one-based index `i+1 ∈ [n]`, the formal bound `n - 1 - ↑i` is the blueprint bound `n - (i+1)`. Thus the theorem establishes precisely that every coordinate of the Lehmer code lies in `H_n`, making the map in part (e) well-defined. `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` faithfully represents permutations of an ordered n-element set, with no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

The target only defines a syntactic word: `Equiv.Perm.Word n` has body `List (Fin (n - 1))`, and `lehmerBlock` constructs the descending list `List.map ... (List.finRange (σ.lehmerEntry i))`. This correctly encodes the sequence of indices and gives an empty list when the Lehmer entry is zero. However, the blueprint also asserts that for zero length “`a_i = id`” and that “`The product a_i equals the cycle (i', i'-1, ..., i)`.” No supplied project definition interprets a `Word` as a permutation, defines its product, or defines the indicated cycle. Thus those parts cannot be stated using the available project definitions; the docstring’s corresponding prose is not a formal assertion. To make the full statement statable and faithful, the project would need a word-evaluation/product definition into `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` together with a cycle definition, followed by a theorem asserting the evaluated `lehmerBlock` is the stated cycle (and the empty block evaluates to the identity).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.no.justification: The body `fun {n} σ => {p | p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.1 < σ p.2}` defines exactly the pairs described informally as “pairs `(i,j)` with `i < j` and `σ(i) < σ(j)`.” The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` faithfully encode `σ ∈ S_n`: `Equiv.Perm` is a bijection from a type to itself, and `Fin n` is the canonical ordered `n`-element type. Using `Fin n = {0,…,n−1}` rather than the blueprint’s `[n] = {1,…,n}` is only an order-preserving reindexing and does not change the notion of non-inversion. The explanatory partition claim is also consistent: injectivity of a permutation ensures that for each pair with `i < j`, exactly one of `σ i < σ j` and `σ i > σ j` holds.

Clause (c) is not faithfully represented. The blueprint says “the directed graph … with arcs i → σ(i),” whereas `cycleDigraph` has codomain `SimpleGraph (Fin n)`, whose adjacency is necessarily symmetric and irreflexive, and its body is `i ≠ j ∧ (σ i = j ∨ σ j = i)`. Thus it forgets arc orientation, adds reverse adjacency, and deletes the loops arising from fixed points. This enters through the target declaration’s `SimpleGraph (Fin n)` codomain and adjacency body. It should instead use a directed-graph structure, or a raw relation with arcs `fun i j => σ i = j`, without `i ≠ j` or the reverse disjunct. Clause (a) is also narrowed: the blueprint permits any ordering `p₁,…,pₙ` of `[n]`, while `twoLineNotation` fixes `List.finRange n` and returns only `[(i, σ i)]`; this is the commonly chosen special case, not the full notion of a two-line notation. To capture the full definition it should accept an ordering/enumeration of `Fin n` and map it to `(p, σ p)`. By contrast, `oneLineNotation` faithfully realizes clause (b) as `List.map σ (List.finRange n)` under the project’s explicit zero-indexed representation `Sn n = Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`.
