stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.pe.justification: The declarations match the components of the blueprint. `Permutation` and `SymmetricGroup` both have body `fun X => Equiv.Perm X`, while `Equiv.Perm` is documented as “the type of bijections from `α` to itself,” matching (a) and the underlying set of the symmetric group in (b); its supplied natural `Group` instance provides the group structure. `symmetricGroup_card` states `Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm X) = (Fintype.card X).factorial`, exactly the claim that its size is `|X|!` when finite. Its extra `[DecidableEq X]` is an implementation/encoding requirement for constructing the relevant `Fintype` instance, not a mathematically substantive restriction. `perm_mul_apply` states `(α * β) x = α (β x)`, matching the composition convention in (c). Finally, `perm_pow_apply` states that natural powers are iterated application, and `perm_zpow_neg_one` states `α ^ (-1) = α⁻¹`, matching the corresponding assertions in (d). Quantifying over arbitrary types rather than only a fixed set is a harmless generalization.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.se.justification: The body `fun {n} σ i j => {a | a < i ∧ σ j < σ a ∧ σ a < σ i}` exactly matches the blueprint formula `A = \{ a < i \mid \sigma (j) < \sigma (a) < \sigma (i)\}`. The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Fin n → Fin n → Finset (Fin n)` correctly encode a permutation of an n-element ordered set and indices `i,j`; using `Fin n` is the zero-based finite-set model corresponding order-isomorphically to the blueprint’s `[n] = {1,…,n}`. Returning a `Finset` rather than a set is appropriate because the domain is finite. No additional mathematically contentful hypothesis restricts the definition.

The body `fun {n} σ i j => {b | j < b ∧ σ j < σ b ∧ σ b < σ i}` exactly matches the defining clause `B = { b > j | σ(j) < σ(b) < σ(i) }`: `b > j` is `j < b`, and the two remaining strict inequalities coincide. The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Fin n → Fin n` encode a permutation of an ordered n-element set and indices in that set; using `Fin n` (zero-based) rather than `[n] = {1,…,n}` is an order-preserving finite-set representation, not a mathematical restriction. The resulting `Finset (Fin n)` is appropriate because the ambient set is finite. No extra hypotheses on `i` or `j` are added. The sentence about paired lost and gained inversions is explanatory context for the set rather than an additional condition in its definition.

The body `fun {n} σ i j => {k | i < k ∧ k < j ∧ σ j < σ k ∧ σ k < σ i}` exactly matches the blueprint’s `Q = { k ∈ { i+1, ..., j-1} | σ(j) < σ(k) < σ(i) }`: membership in `{i+1, ..., j-1}` is expressed by `i < k ∧ k < j`, and the image inequalities are expressed by `σ j < σ k ∧ σ k < σ i`. The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Fin n → Fin n` appropriately model a permutation and indices of a finite ordered set, while the `Finset (Fin n)` result represents the finite set Q. No additional mathematical hypothesis or narrowed quantifier is introduced.

The formal body `fun {n} σ i j => {k | i < k ∧ k < j ∧ σ i < σ k ∧ σ k < σ j}` exactly represents the blueprint’s `R = { k ∈ { i+1, ..., j-1} | σ(i) < σ(k) < σ(j) }`: for `k : Fin n`, membership in `{i+1, …, j-1}` is equivalently `i < k ∧ k < j`, and the remaining conjuncts express the two strict image inequalities. The binders `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Fin n → Fin n` supply precisely a finite permutation and indices; they add no mathematically contentful hypothesis.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.si.justification: The blueprint states: “Let n ∈ ℕ and i ∈ [n−1]” and defines “s_i := t_{i,i+1} ∈ S_n.” The formal definition quantifies `{n : ℕ}` and `i : Fin (n - 1)`, with body `Equiv.swap ⟨↑i, ⋯⟩ ⟨↑i + 1, ⋯⟩`. Since `AlgebraicCombinatorics.Sn n` is `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` and `AlgebraicCombinatorics.transposition` is defined as `Equiv.swap`, this is exactly the transposition of the two adjacent represented elements. The use of `Fin n = {0,…,n−1}` instead of the textbook `[n] = {1,…,n}` is the project’s documented zero-based encoding: formal `i.val` represents the textbook index `i+1`, so the adjacent pair is preserved under the shift. The theorem `simpleTransposition_eq_transposition` explicitly gives the defining equality, while the two application lemmas and `simpleTransposition_apply_of_ne` correctly record that the endpoints are exchanged and every other element is fixed. Natural subtraction causes no mismatch at `n = 0` or `n = 1`, because both the informal index set `[n−1]` and the formal type `Fin (n−1)` are empty there.

The blueprint defines the integer sign by “the integer $(-1)^{\ell(\sigma)}$,” where $\ell(\sigma)$ is the number of inversions. The first target states exactly the corresponding integer equality: `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)), ↑(Equiv.Perm.sign σ) = (-1) ^ AlgebraicCombinatorics.Perm.invCount σ`. Here `invCount σ` unfolds to `(inv σ).card`, and `inv σ` unfolds to the pairs satisfying `p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.1 > σ p.2`, exactly matching the informal definition of inversions and length. The coercion `↑(Equiv.Perm.sign σ)` is the underlying integer value of the unit returned by Mathlib’s sign. The second target gives the same equality internally in `ℤˣ`. There are no added mathematical hypotheses: the only binders are `{n : ℕ}` and `σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`, matching `$n\in\mathbb N$` and `$\sigma\in S_n$`. Using the canonically ordered `Fin n = {0,…,n-1}` rather than the informal `[n]={1,…,n}` is an equivalent indexing convention and does not alter inversion count or restrict the permutations covered.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.sm.justification: The body `fun {n} σ i => {j | j < i ∧ σ j < σ i}.card` exactly gives the cardinality in the blueprint’s `|{ j < i : σ(j) < σ(i) }|`. The binders `σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` and `i : Fin n` encode `σ ∈ S_n` and `i ∈ [n]`: `Equiv.Perm` is a bijection from the set to itself, while `Fin n` is the canonical n-element ordered type. Although `Fin n` is zero-based whereas the informal `[n]` is `{1,…,n}`, the order-preserving shift identifies them and preserves both inequalities, so the count is unchanged. Restricting `n` to `ℕ` causes no substantive loss: for informal negative `n`, `[n]` is empty and hence there is no `i ∈ [n]` at which this definition must produce a value.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.sn.justification: The blueprint begins, “Let $n \in \mathbb Z$,” and defines $[n]$ for negative indices as well: it “is an empty set if $n \le 0$.” By contrast, both defining declarations have the restricted binder `ℕ → Type`: `bracketN` is `fun n => Fin n`, and `Sn` is `fun n => Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`. Thus they cannot even take a negative integer index, so the blueprint’s definitions of `[n]` and `S_n` for `n < 0` are omitted. This is a mathematically contentful narrowing from integers to naturals, not merely an encoding detail. The shift from `{1,…,n}` to `Fin n = {0,…,n-1}` is otherwise a harmless finite-set representation, and `sn_card : ∀ (n : ℕ), Fintype.card (Sn n) = n.factorial` faithfully covers the blueprint’s cardinality claim “when $n \ge 0$.” To make the package faithful, the index binder of `bracketN` and consequently `Sn` should range over integers, with `bracketN n` representing `{i \in \mathbb Z \mid 1 \le i \land i \le n}` (hence empty for negative `n`), while the cardinality theorem should quantify over integer `n` subject to `0 ≤ n` and compare with the factorial of the corresponding natural number.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.ti.justification: The formalization defines `transposition i j` as `Equiv.swap i j`, whose documented meaning is the permutation that “swaps `a` and `b` and leaves other values as is.” The three theorems exactly provide the stated behavior: `(transposition i j) i = j`, `(transposition i j) j = i`, and, under `x ≠ i → x ≠ j`, `(transposition i j) x = x`. Although the blueprint assumes “`i` and `j` [are] two distinct elements,” the formal binders impose no `i ≠ j`; this makes the declarations strictly more general, and they imply the blueprint statement by specialization to distinct `i,j`. The `[DecidableEq X]` binder is the computational instance required by `Equiv.swap`, encoding the formal construction rather than a mathematically contentful alteration of the transposition claim.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.perm.wo.justification: The body `fun n => List (Fin (n - 1))` exactly represents finite sequences of indices in the stated range. By the library definitions, `List` gives a finite ordered sequence and `Fin (n - 1)` consists of naturals `k < n - 1`, i.e. `k ∈ {0, 1, …, n-2}`. Natural subtraction saturates at zero, so the small cases `n = 0` and `n = 1` correctly admit no indices. Although `q` is not a parameter of `Word`, each list has a definite finite length `q`, matching the statement’s parenthetical “of length q” rather than restricting the type to one fixed length.

The target takes `{n : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm.Word n → Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`, and `Equiv.Perm.Word n` is exactly `List (Fin (n - 1))`, matching a finite sequence of indices in `{0, …, n-2}`. Its body `(List.map Equiv.Perm.simpleTransposition w).prod` maps `w = (k₁, …, k_q)` to the corresponding simple transpositions and multiplies them in list order. By `List.prod`, this is `s_{k₁} * (s_{k₂} * ⋯ * (s_{k_q} * 1))`, hence the stated product `s_{k₁}s_{k₂}⋯s_{k_q}` under the informal convention that permutation multiplication is composition. The dependency `simpleTransposition` swaps the positions indexed by `k` and `k+1`, so it realizes the required `s_k`. The empty and small-`n` cases are also consistent because `Fin (n - 1)` is empty when there are no simple-transposition indices.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pie.der.justification: The target defines, for every type `α`, the subtype `{ σ // ∀ (x : α), σ x ≠ x }`, where `σ` is a permutation (`Equiv.Perm α`, whose docstring says it is a bijection from `α` to itself). Thus its elements are exactly permutations of `α` satisfying “for every `x`, `σ x ≠ x`,” i.e. having no fixed points. This matches the blueprint: “a permutation of `X` that has no fixed points.” Representing the underlying set `X` by its carrier type `α` introduces no mathematically substantive restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pie.num.justification: The blueprint definition fixes `[n]` for every integer: “Let $n \in \mathbb Z$” and says it is empty when $n \le 0$. Thus `numSurj(m,n)` is intended to cover integer indices, including negative `m` or `n`. The target instead has the restricted binders `ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`, so it defines the count only for natural `m,n`; this narrowed domain is a contentful restriction. On nonnegative inputs, using `Fin m` and `Fin n` rather than `{1,…,m}` and `{1,…,n}` does not alter the number of surjections, since these finite sets are bijective. To be faithful, the target should accept integer indices and represent `[k]` as empty for `k ≤ 0` (equivalently, use a nonnegative-size conversion before taking the corresponding finite type), or the informal statement must explicitly restrict `m,n` to natural/nonnegative integers.
